title: Long-term effect of early-life stress from earthquake exposure on working memory in adulthood.
ehr_evidence: The questionnaires and psychological evaluation were finished using a one-on-one method involving the study subjects and investigators who received unified training.
summary: A cohort study of 907 adults born and raised in Tangshan examining the long-term effect of 1976 Tangshan earthquake early-life exposure on working memory (visuospatial memory) in adulthood.
key_findings: BVMT-R total scores were significantly lower in the infant exposure group compared with the no-exposure group (P=0.006), indicating impaired visuospatial memory.
HVLT-R scores showed no significant difference across the three exposure groups (P>0.05), indicating verbal learning was unaffected.
Among prenatal subgroups, second and third trimester exposure had significantly lower BVMT-R total scores than first trimester (P=0.038).
Education level (OR=2.289, 95% CI=1.435–3.650, P<0.001) and earthquake exposure (OR=1.437, 95% CI=1.061–1.947, P=0.019) were independent risk factors for impaired visuospatial memory.
Physical neglect (P<0.001), emotional abuse (P=0.021), and sexual abuse (P=0.018) were associated with reduced visuospatial memory performance.
pathologies_diseases: impaired visuospatial memory (reduced working memory performance)
population: 907 adults (mean age ~37–38 years) born and raised in Tangshan, recruited from Kailuan Mining Group workers
exposure_domain: early-life stress from earthquake exposure (natural disaster)
limitations: Earthquake and pregnancy information was obtained retrospectively from parents or insiders, introducing recall bias.
No neuroimaging or biological studies were performed to explore underlying mechanisms.
Potential confounders (genetic background, adult life events, lifestyle, diet, alcohol, drug abuse) could not be quantitatively analyzed.
Small sample size limits statistical power.
